passage: Shreya, you're going to your first big concert on Saturday, so let your old music teacher tell you something. It was the happiest night, and honestly, half that happiness came from the people around me. Then, at the end, somebody at the gate shouted and the crowd surged, and the fear arrived just as fast. subtype: Setting the tone of a team [Response]
passage: The kitchen at the hotel goes quiet in a particular way when the head of the line is in a bad mood. I learned that last winter. On one busy Friday Saurabh dropped a stack of plates right after I snapped at him, and the young cook beside him burned the onions. Later, washing up, Saurabh said, 'Sonali di, when you're tense, we all go tense. We're watching your face.' That stung. It was also true. Now, before service, I stand at the pass, take one slow breath and say something honest: 'Big night, we're short one person, we'll get through it.' I still feel the pressure. I just stopped throwing it at them. The plates break less now. Mostly.

passage: When I moved to the new school in Class 9, I didn't tell anyone anything for months. He was funny and kind, but kind people can still talk. So I tested him. I told him I can't swim, and that I get out of every pool trip by saying I have a cold. Small, embarrassing, nothing huge. I waited. A pool trip came and went, and nobody teased me. Pankaj even said, 'Uma, want to skip together and eat chaat?' A month later I told him the real thing, that my parents were separating. He listened and didn't tell a soul. I'm glad I went slowly. I'm also glad I didn't stop at the first step.

subtype: Trusting and being let down [Receiver]
passage: Bhupen spent six weeks on his botany project at the college in Tezpur, walking the tea-garden edges every morning to count ferns. Alka, from the next village bus stop, asked to see his draft. 'Just to get the format right,' she said. He sent it the same night. At the seminar, Alka presented first. Her slides had his fern counts, his map, even his joke about the goat eating a sample. Bhupen sat very still while the teacher praised her. On the bus home he watched the paddy fields and felt like a fool. For a week he didn't reply to anyone's messages. Then his friend Moni asked for help with graphs. He almost said no. Instead he helped her in the library, where the teacher could see, and kept his own files dated. He hadn't stopped helping. He'd just started helping more carefully.

qa.q: What did Alka ask Bhupen for?
qa.a: Alka asked to see his draft, 'just to get the format right'.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel on the bus home after the seminar?
qa.a: He felt betrayed and like a fool for trusting Alka, sitting silent and watching the paddy fields.

qa.q: What choice did Bhupen make when Moni asked for help, and why was it a good one?
qa.a: He helped her, but in the library where the teacher could see and with his own files dated, so he stayed generous while protecting his work.

qa.q: How might Moni be affected if Bhupen had decided never to share again?
qa.a: Moni, who had done nothing wrong, would have lost help with her graphs because of what Alka did.

grounding: A student whose project draft is copied feels betrayed and gullible, then learns to share more carefully instead of refusing to trust anyone.

subtype: Trusting and being let down [Receiver]
passage: In their shared flat in Lisbon, Chidi lent Paulo two hundred euros in September. Paulo said his scholarship payment was late and he'd return it in a fortnight. November came. Paulo bought concert tickets, posted photos from a weekend trip, and changed the subject whenever Chidi mentioned money. One evening Chidi sat on his narrow bed, looking at his bank app, feeling foolish. His mother had always said he trusted too easily. Maybe she was right. Maybe he should trust no one. The next week a classmate, Lucía, asked to borrow his lecture notes before an exam. Chidi hesitated, then said yes, and added, 'Can I have them back Thursday?' She returned them Wednesday, with a thank-you chocolate. Chidi smiled. He still wanted the money back from Paulo. But one person had not decided who everyone else was.

qa.q: How much did Chidi lend Paulo?
qa.a: Chidi lent Paulo two hundred euros in September.

qa.q: What was Chidi feeling when he sat on his bed looking at his bank app?
qa.a: He felt foolish and betrayed, and wondered whether his mother was right that he trusted too easily.

qa.q: What did Chidi do differently when Lucía asked for his notes, and why did it work?
qa.a: He lent them but asked for them back by Thursday, trusting her with a clear limit, and she returned them early.

qa.q: How might Lucía have been treated if Chidi had decided to trust no one?
qa.a: Lucía might have been refused the notes before her exam, even though she had done nothing to deserve suspicion.

grounding: A student let down over an unpaid loan feels gullible, and then chooses to trust more carefully, with clear limits, rather than trust no one.

subtype: Reputation travels through others [Observer]
passage: In her first week at the Pune office, Usha hadn't met half her team. But she already knew things about them. At the coffee machine, a senior said, 'Give it to Imran. He'll have it done by evening.' In the lift, two people groaned about another colleague: 'Don't put him on anything with a deadline.' Usha hadn't worked with either. On Thursday she finally sat with Imran on a small task. She watched him reply to every message within the hour, write down each thing he promised, and send a two-line update before leaving. Nothing dramatic. Just the same small thing, every day. On the bus home Usha thought about her own first week: the email she'd forgotten to answer, the meeting she'd been five minutes late to. Somewhere, someone was already describing her.

qa.q: What did the senior say at the coffee machine?
qa.a: The senior said, 'Give it to Imran. He'll have it done by evening.'

qa.q: What was Usha thinking about on the bus home?
qa.a: She felt uneasy thinking about her own first week, the forgotten email and being late, and realised someone was already describing her too.

qa.q: What small choice could Usha make next week, based on what she saw?
qa.a: She could answer emails within the hour and send short updates like Imran, so her small daily actions build the reputation she wants.

qa.q: How might the colleague people groaned about feel if he knew what was said in the lift?
qa.a: He would likely feel hurt and judged by people who may not even have worked with him, and it would be hard to change the story.

grounding: A new employee hears colleagues pass on who is reliable before she has worked with them and sees that reputations grow from small consistent actions.

subtype: Reputation travels through others [Observer]
passage:
'Lavanya, a word before you pick your shifts.'
'Sure, Sarika.'
'Take Dr Menon's night shifts if you can. She actually explains.'
'I haven't met her yet.'

'And Dr Rao?'
'Nice man. But double-check everything he signs. Twice.'
'Has he done something wrong?'
'Not big. Small things. A missed dose chart, a late handover. Everyone knows.'
'That's... a lot to know about someone I've never seen.'
'Welcome to the hospital. By next month, people will be saying things about you too.'
'Like what?'
'Like whether you finish your notes before handover. Whether you answer the ward phone.'
Lavanya looked down at her clipboard, at the notes she hadn't finished yet. 'Okay. Then I'd better finish these.'
Sarika laughed. 'See? You're learning faster than Rao.'

subtype: Reputation travels through others [Observer]
passage: Before I met Chinmay, I already knew three things about him. My name's Hafsa, and I had just joined the architecture firm as a junior. On my first day, the office manager said, 'If you're stuck, ask Chinmay, he never says he'll do something and forgets.' The receptionist said his drawings always arrived on time. And in the pantry, someone said a different colleague 'means well but you have to chase him'. It was strange. I hadn't worked with any of them. By the time I did work with Chinmay, a month later, he was exactly as described: small promises, all kept. What stayed with me was how quietly it had all travelled. Nobody sent a memo. It just moved from person to person over tea. So now I reply the same day, even if it's just 'got it, will send by Friday.' I know someone is passing me on.

qa.q: What did the receptionist say about Chinmay?
qa.a: The receptionist said his drawings always arrived on time.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa find it strange to know so much about colleagues already?
qa.a: Hafsa felt surprised to know so much before working with any of them, and was struck by how quietly it had all travelled over tea.

qa.q: What change did Hafsa make after seeing how reputations move, and why?
qa.a: Hafsa now replies the same day, even with a short 'got it', knowing that small kept promises are what people pass on.

qa.q: How might the colleague who 'means well but you have to chase him' be affected by this talk?
qa.a: He may find that new juniors already expect to chase him, which makes it harder to be seen fresh even if he tries to change.

grounding: A junior architect learns about colleagues' reliability through office talk before working with them and realises reputation spreads informally from small kept promises.

subtype: Repairing broken trust [Response]
passage: I'm Karthik. Asif and I have run the tiffin service together for two years. Last spring he spent the rent money we'd kept aside, and the landlord came knocking. I found out from the landlord, not from him. That night Asif came to my room and said, 'I took it. I didn't tell you. That was wrong.' No excuses. He set up a repayment from his share, a bit each month, and gave me the account password. Then he just kept showing up. Six-thirty every morning, every delivery logged, every rupee in the notebook. For months I was cold with him. He never once asked, 'Are we okay now?' I don't know what it cost him inside. I only know that last week, without really thinking, I handed him the cash box for the weekend. He took it and nodded, and neither of us said anything.

qa.q: Who did Karthik find out about the rent money from?
qa.a: Karthik found out from the landlord, not from Asif.

qa.q: What does Asif never asking 'Are we okay now?' suggest about him?
qa.a: It suggests he understood that trust had to come back through his actions, and he didn't want to pressure Karthik into forgiving him.

qa.q: Which of Asif's choices did most to rebuild trust, and why?
qa.a: Showing up at six-thirty and logging every delivery and rupee for months gave Karthik repeated proof, which mattered more than the apology alone.

qa.q: How might Karthik have felt in the months of being cold with Asif?
qa.a: Karthik probably felt hurt and wary, wanting to believe Asif but needing time and evidence before relaxing again.

grounding: A business partner watches a friend who broke their trust admit it plainly, repay it, and act reliably for months without asking to be forgiven, until trust slowly returns.

subtype: Repairing broken trust [Response]
passage:
Day one: in the client meeting, Akash presented the café logo as his idea. It was Jahnavi's. She said nothing, just closed her laptop. That evening he called her. 'I took credit for your work. I'm sorry. I'll fix it with the client.' The next morning he emailed the client: the concept was Jahnavi's.
Six weeks later: Akash mentioned Jahnavi's name first in every review. He sent her his drafts before meetings. When she was still short with him, he didn't argue or say, 'I already apologised.' He kept doing it.
Four months on: the studio got a new bakery account. Jahnavi read the brief and turned to him. 'Want to pitch this with me?' Akash noticed she was waiting to see how he'd handle it. 'Your concept, your name first,' he said. She nodded, and for the first time in months, she smiled at him properly.

qa.q: Whose idea was the café logo?
qa.a: It was Jahnavi's.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling when she closed her laptop in the meeting?
qa.a: She was likely hurt and angry that Akash had taken credit for her work, but chose to say nothing then.

qa.q: What did Akash do after his apology that helped rebuild trust?
qa.a: He corrected it with the client, put her name first in every review and shared drafts, and he kept doing it without demanding forgiveness.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt when Jahnavi asked him to pitch with her?
qa.a: Akash may have felt relieved but careful, knowing she was waiting to see how he'd handle it, so he put her concept and name first.

grounding: A young designer who took credit for a colleague's idea admits it, makes amends and behaves fairly for months, and trust returns slowly through evidence.

subtype: Repairing broken trust [Response]
passage: Chandrika, beti, you broke your friend's trust and now you want her to forgive you by Sunday. Let your Sachin Mama tell you something. When I was twenty-five, I was treasurer of our building society in Nashik. I forgot to pay the water bill three months running, and one morning the tank was dry. Forty families, no water. I went door to door. 'It was me. I forgot. I'm sorry.' I paid the fine from my own salary. Then for two years, I pinned the receipt on the notice board the day each bill was paid. Some neighbours stayed cool with me for a year. Mrs Kulkarni wouldn't even nod. I didn't chase her. One Diwali she sent sweets and asked me to handle the festival fund. Two years, beti. Trust comes back one receipt at a time. Say sorry, yes. Then show her, again and again.

qa.q: How many families were left without water?
qa.a: Forty families had no water.

qa.q: How might Sachin Mama have felt when Mrs Kulkarni wouldn't nod for a year?
qa.a: He probably felt hurt and uncomfortable, but he accepted that she needed time and chose not to chase her.

qa.q: What would you advise Chandrika, based on Sachin Mama's story?
qa.a: Apologise plainly, then keep showing reliable behaviour to her friend for a long stretch, without pushing her to forgive by Sunday.

qa.q: How did Mrs Kulkarni's view of Sachin change over time?
qa.a: At first she wouldn't even nod, but after two years of receipts on the board she trusted him enough to ask him to handle the festival fund.

grounding: An uncle tells his niece how he admitted a failure plainly, made amends and stayed reliable for years without demanding forgiveness until trust slowly returned.
